# CLAUDE.md

This file provides guidance to Claude Code (claude.ai/code) when working with code in this repository.

## House rules & tooling

The house **directives** that govern every change in this project — architect mentality, **architecture-first**, the **branch & release rules**, and **a feature is a package** — are imported on the line below, so they are **always in context**. They are **mandatory, not optional reference.**

@HOUSE.rules.md

The **mechanical how-to** — the stack · generators · Nx — lives in **[`HOUSE.md`](HOUSE.md)**. **Read it before you branch, or reach for a house command.**

Both files are **generator-owned**, regenerated on every `house.sh upgrade` to match the installed `@bespunky/nx-tools`. **Never hand-edit them** — this project's own guidance goes below, outside these markers.
<!-- @bespunky/house-tooling:end -->

## What this repo is

`claude-toolkit` is a **Claude Code plugin marketplace** — a git repo whose product is **skills** (and, where added, subagents/commands) authored as markdown. There is no application and no root build: editing a skill *is* the work. `README.md` holds the exhaustive plugin/skill catalog and the install/upgrade story; this file is the map for **developing the toolkit itself**.

The repo is also its own **local marketplace**: `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json` lists every plugin with a **relative** `./plugins/...` source, so `claude plugin marketplace add .` loads the plugins live from the working tree. The devcontainer's `.devcontainer/post-create.sh` does exactly this on build, so your edits are live in-session (dogfooding).

## Architecture (the big picture)

**Marketplace → plugins → skills.**
- `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json` (repo root) — the registry: one entry per plugin (`name`, relative `source`, `version`).
- `plugins/<plugin>/.claude-plugin/plugin.json` — the plugin manifest (`name`, `description`, `version`).
- `plugins/<plugin>/skills/<skill>/SKILL.md` — a skill. Subagents go at `plugins/<plugin>/agents/<name>.md`, slash commands at `plugins/<plugin>/commands/<name>.md`, hooks at `plugins/<plugin>/hooks/hooks.json`.

**Hooks are the "runs without being chosen" escape hatch.** A skill only fires when Claude judges it relevant, and there is **no plugin-install/update hook event** at all — so anything that must happen *reliably* (not "if the model thinks to") needs a hook. A plugin's hooks run in the sessions of everyone who has that plugin **installed**, i.e. in the consumer's project, not here. `house` uses this: a `SessionStart` hook orders the stamp in the project's `HOUSE.md` header against the installed `@bespunky/nx-tools` version and, when the toolkit has moved on, tells Claude to offer an upgrade (`/bespunky-house:upgrade`).

Three rules that hook earned the hard way, and that any new hook should keep:
- **Detect, don't execute.** It *relays a fact*; it never runs the upgrade (Docker, minutes, rewrites files). A hook that commands the model to act is one compliant model away from doing the thing you refused to automate — and in a headless run there is no one to consent.
- **Compare what actually drives the output** (`nx-tools`, where the generators live) — *not* the plugin version, which this repo's own convention bumps for a README typo. A notice that fires when nothing would change is a notice everyone learns to ignore.
- **A stamp is a repo fact; an install is a machine fact.** Order them, don't just diff them: "the project is ahead of this machine" is an ordinary state (a teammate who hasn't updated), and treating it as staleness would push an upgrade that *downgrades* the project. And keep the stamp somewhere unambiguously committed — `.claude/` is where *local* state lives, so a stamp there is one `.gitignore` line from vanishing.

**The `description` frontmatter of a SKILL.md is load-bearing** — it is the *only* text Claude sees when deciding whether to fire the skill. Writing/editing that description is designing the trigger; it matters as much as the body. Skills cross-reference each other by namespaced id `bespunky-<plugin>:<skill>` (e.g. `bespunky-engineering:architecture-first`).

**Two skill shapes:**
- **Standalone** — a single SKILL.md carries the whole thing.
- **Router / domain skills** — SKILL.md is only an *index* of technique clusters; the depth lives in sibling `reference/*.md` files loaded **on demand** (progressive disclosure). When editing these, keep SKILL.md thin (routing + when-to-use) and put substance in the reference files. Most of `engineering` and the `product-ux` visual skills (`astonishing-to-use`, `stage-the-vision`, `realize-the-vision`) follow this shape.

**The "always-on half" pattern (consumer-facing).** A skill only fires when judged relevant — insufficient for a mindset/rule that must hold on *every* change. So `engineering`'s `architect-mentality` + `architecture-first` (and `product-ux`'s `redesign-means-rethink`) are paired with **always-on directives** the house engine bakes into a consumer project's generated `HOUSE.rules.md`, which its `CLAUDE.md` imports. The canonical directive text lives in `README.md` ("The always-on half") and in `house-doc/HOUSE.rules.md.tpl` — if you change those skills' contract, update that text with it.

**The branch model is a DECLARED project fact, never a toolkit assumption.** A consumer's `.bespunky/branches.json` says which lines exist (integration, a staged chain, release/hotfix lines, maintained versions) and how each advances; the copy on the integration line's tip is the one in force. **One engine interprets it** — `workflow`'s `skills/branch-and-release/scripts/branches.mjs` (read-only git by construction; it plans moves, never executes them) — and writes a flat, derived `projection` block that is the **only** part the other readers may parse. There are exactly **two resolvers** (which copy of the file is in force, and the undeclared/unreadable fallbacks): the engine itself and its bash counterpart for the engine's preflight, `plugins/house/engine/house-branches.sh`. Everyone else consumes one of them: the PreCompact hook calls `branches.mjs status --json`; house-doc is **handed** the resolved projection by the upgrade (its `branchProjection` option, from the preflight) and reads the `Tree` itself only when run standalone. Same split as `layers.sh` from the layer registry, and for the same reason: three update channels (auto-updating plugin, per-project pinned `nx-tools`, bash) must never each carry the semantics. Nothing writes the file without a human decision — no generator, no migration, no upgrade. The one narrow exception is a **format-only migration the user explicitly approved**, which rewrites how a declared fact is spelled without changing what it declares or the projection (0.50.0 `deploys-object-form`: a bare-string `deploys` → `{ "note": … }`); the engine reports such an outdated spelling in `status`'s notes and refuses it in `describe`/`verify`/`write`, so a project that has not upgraded is told the exact rewrite. That is not a model change — never stretch it to one. An undeclared project protects every branch the toolkit ever forced and Claude investigates and **asks**. Spec and the reasoning: `docs/features/2026-10-03-branch-model/`.

## `house` is special — it carries the engine

Most plugins are pure markdown. `house` (`bespunky-house`; renamed from `project-starter` — see `docs/features/2026-10-03-house-plugin-rename/`) also ships an executable **engine** under `plugins/house/engine/`, which its commands (`/bespunky-house:upgrade`, `/bespunky-house:add-layer`) and its `new` skill drive:
- `house.sh <new|upgrade|add-layer> [flags] …` — thin launcher; the subcommand comes first, flags before positionals. Runs the generators on the **local Node** when it's 22.18+, falling back to the `typescript-node` base image via `docker run` only for an old host Node. `house.sh new [--preset=<id>] [--add-layer=<csv>] <project> [app]` creates; a bare `house.sh new <project>` is the **`agent` preset** (the house DX on the Nx floor — no `package.json`, no Angular, no app); the Angular house app that used to be the default is `new --preset=angular [--firebase] [--staging] <project> [app]`. `house.sh upgrade [--local] <project>` brings an existing project up to the current house standard: **probe → floor → install → migrate → detect → generate** — and adds **no** layer (it refuses `--add-layer`/`--preset`/`--firebase`). `house.sh add-layer [--preset=<id>] [--firebase] [--local] <layers-csv> <project>` is that same upgrade with an ensure set. Each command's name says what it does.
- **Upgrade is MIGRATIONS + generators, not convergence.** It used to be convergence alone: every generator re-ran and re-asserted desired state, which meant each one carried unbounded *legacy healing* — code that had to recognise every shape the toolkit had ever produced, forever, so that a project three versions behind still landed on the current one. That doesn't scale, and it made every generator a museum. Now a one-way change ships as a **versioned migration** at `engine/nx-tools/src/migrations/<version>/<name>.ts`, registered in `engine/nx-tools/migrations.json` and exposed through the `nx-migrations` key of the payload's `package.json`, so **native `nx migrate`** collects and orders them. Two consequences that shape everything around it:
  - **`@bespunky/nx-tools` is a real, exactly-pinned npm devDependency** — no longer copied into `node_modules`. The copy is what made migrations impossible: `nx migrate` decides what a project needs by reading the version *resolved out of `node_modules`*, and a copy always read the new one, so the ladder was always empty. For the same reason the pin is exact, never a caret: a floated install would move that version with no migration behind it. **`--local` packs the working tree (`npm pack`) and installs that** — the same real install, different origin — which is how a toolkit change is tested before it reaches npm, on this repo included.
  - **A PROBE runs first — before anything is written — and the migrations run after the install, with an explicit `--from`.** Order: **probe** → lay the Nx floor (if missing) → install → **migrate** → detect layers → generators → `house-doc` **last** (it writes the stamp, so it must see the final layer set). The probe comes before `nx init`, not merely before the install, because its refusal claims to fire *before anything is written* — and the always-ensured floor would otherwise have created `nx.json` (and, on the node host, a lockfile) in someone's repo before the upgrade decided it should not run at all. The probe answers *where is this project actually at* from two sources — the version resolved in `node_modules` (or `.nx/installation` on the wrapper host) and the `nx-tools=` version stamped in `HOUSE.md` — and takes the **older** of the two as the migration floor. Not caution for its own sake: every project scaffolded before this release declares a **caret** range, so an ordinary `yarn install` has already floated `node_modules` to the newest published version with **no migration having run**. Trust that number alone and the upgrade concludes "already current", collects nothing, and lets `house-doc` stamp the gap closed — permanently, because the stamp is then the lie that every later upgrade believes. The same two numbers answer the opposite question with the **newer** of them: if *either* source says this project has been above the version this checkout installs, the upgrade **refuses before the install** — that is a downgrade, and migrations do not walk backwards, so there is no repair path. The ladder then runs with an **explicit `--from`** taken from the probe, and that is precisely what freed the ordering: the range no longer depends on whatever happens to be resolved in `node_modules`, so the install can safely come first.
- **Three classes of generator output, and knowing which is which is how you decide where a change belongs.** **(A) Owned template artifacts** — shared-browser, worktree-domains, `house-doc`/`HOUSE.md`, `post-create.sh`, a devcontainer the generator owns, **and the house-owned targets and keys inside a project's configuration** (the targets a house project's generator declares, `firebase.json`'s `emulators`/`functions`) — are re-asserted every upgrade; change them in the generator. Ownership is per key, not per file: a `project.json` or `firebase.json` holds both kinds side by side. **(B) Project state** — what the *project* added: its own targets (and what it added inside an owned one), its dependencies, the other `firebase.json` keys, env files — is created at baseline and thereafter evolved **only by a migration**; a generator must preserve it, never reshape it. Renaming or retiring an owned target is therefore still a migration: the generator only states the new shape, and the old one stays behind in every existing project until a rung removes it. **(C) Seeded but never owned** — design tokens, `environment.ts`, `ds-theme`, `post-create.local.sh` — is written once and never again, because it is precisely what the project is expected to replace.
- **The engine is LAYERED, and that is its central idea.** A project is a stack of layers — `nx` (the floor), `agent` (stack-agnostic DX), `node`, `js`, `web`, `angular`, `design-system`, `navigation`, `firebase` — each **detected from the workspace**. Two questions kept strictly apart: **detect** (what the workspace has — read, never declared) and **ensure** (the *ensure set*: `add-layer <csv>` / `new --add-layer=<csv>`, or a `--preset=<id>`, a named ensure set; the two union — what this run should create, always explicit; `upgrade` ensures **nothing above the Nx floor**, which is why it is its own command).
  - **The layer registry is the single source of truth.** One file per layer, `nx-tools/src/layers/<id>.ts`, exporting a `LayerDescriptor` — evidence, `requires`, ensurability (per run mode — the descriptor's `new` and `upgrade` keys, the latter covering `add-layer`, each `true`/`false` or `via` another layer), the hint a human acts on, generator steps (`workspace` and per-`app`), its devcontainer fragment, its `HOUSE.md`/`HOUSE.rules.md` sections, the Claude plugins it enables — registered in `layers/registry.ts` in dependency order (validated at load). Every generator's `requireLayer()` guard, the planner (`layers/cli.js plan`), house-doc and the devcontainer composer read it. `engine/layers.sh` is its **generated** pure-bash projection for the two readers that cannot load the package — `house.sh` (it validates the ensure set before anything is installed) and the `SessionStart` hook — regenerated by `node tools/test-layers/run.mjs --write`; drift fails CI. **Adding a layer:** write the descriptor, register it after everything it requires, regenerate `layers.sh`, add a `tools/test-layers` case — `house.sh`, `--help`, the hook and house-doc follow with no further edit. **Presets** are data beside the registry (`layers/presets.ts`: `agent` — the default —, `node`, `angular`), validated closed under `requires` and projected into `layers.sh` the same way; adding one is one entry plus the regenerate.
  - **The Nx floor is always ensured, and it is not "be a Node project".** A repo without `nx.json` gets `nx init` in place. With a `package.json` that is the **node host** (Nx and the toolkit as exact devDependencies, through the project's package manager); without one it is the **wrapper host** — `./nx`, `.nx/nxw.js`, the toolkit and `@nx/devkit` pinned exactly in `nx.json` → `installation.plugins` — and the repo gains no `package.json`, lockfile or `node_modules`. House docs render Nx commands as `./nx` there. `@nx/devkit` is installed on the node host because an `nx init` workspace doesn't ship it.
  - **Stacks are adapters, everything else is a capability.** A stack (`nx-tools/src/adapters/`: `angular`, `js`; registry `ADAPTERS`) builds things — apps, libs, env files, providers, styles, dev-server ports. A capability (`firebase`, `design-system`, `navigation`, `web`) does its framework-neutral part itself and reaches an app **only through that app's adapter's ports**. **Adding a stack:** one `adapters/<id>.ts` with the ports it can honour, registered in `ADAPTERS`, plus its layer — no capability generator changes. `publishable-lib --stack=<adapter>` is the library entry (`--nonAngular` is a deprecated alias of `--stack=js`), and the `app` generator creates through the adapter (`--stack`) and then runs every active layer's per-app steps — the same steps an upgrade runs.
  - **The workspace SHAPE is two more detected facts — layout and linking — orthogonal to the layers and to each other.** **Layout** (where projects live: `apps-libs`, `packages`, default `apps/` + `packages/`) is `_utils/workspace-layout.ts` — `nx.json` `workspaceLayout` → inferred from existing projects (`tools/` excluded) → default. **Linking** (how projects reach each other) is ONE PORT, `_utils/linking/` (`link` / `resolve` / `importPathOf` / `unlink`), with two strategies: `paths` (project.json + tsconfig aliases) and `workspaces` (Nx TS-solution: package.json projects, PM workspaces, project references, consumers declaring `workspace:*` / `*`), picked by our own copy of Nx's `isUsingTsSolutionSetup` (it is only exported from `@nx/js/internal`). Which file defines a project is `_utils/project-files.ts`. Same split as layers: **`new` chooses** (`--layout`, `--linking`; omitted = the old output exactly), **`upgrade`/`add-layer` refuse both flags and detect** — so no existing project changes shape, and there is nothing to migrate. **Never hardcode `apps/`, `libs/` or a tsconfig alias in a generator or a house-doc template** — resolve the layout, go through the linking port, render `{{APPS_DIR}}` / `{{LIBS_DIR}}`. **Angular in a TS-solution workspace rides an undocumented upstream opt-out** (`NX_IGNORE_UNSUPPORTED_TS_SETUP`, which `@nx/angular`'s `assertNotUsingTsSolutionSetup` honours), set for ONE awaited generator call at a time by the seam `adapters/angular/ts-solution.ts` and nowhere else; Angular apps are `project.json` islands, Angular libs real workspace packages. If Nx renames or drops the variable, every guarded call fails loudly with Nx's own error — the generator fixture test (TS-solution + Angular) is the tripwire, so keep it in CI and re-check it on every Nx bump.
  - **The dev loop is stack-free.** `.bespunky/dev.json` declares what a project serves (processes, ports); the generator-owned `tools/dev/dev serve` (Node built-ins only) runs it — worktree selection, port offset, `<slug>.localhost`, the shared browser, one Ctrl+C. `nx serve <app>` is a thin wrapper over it (kebab-case flags: `--worktree=`, `--port-offset=`, `--skip=`, `--no-shared-browser`, `--no-emulators`, `--configuration=`); a Python or Go repo writes `dev.json` by hand and wears the `web` layer all the same.
  - **The devcontainer is composed, not templated.** Each active layer's fragment (image, features, mounts, env, OS packages, post-create pieces) is composed into `devcontainer.json`, one `post-create.sh`, and the image the container is BUILT from — `.devcontainer/house.Dockerfile` (FROM the composed image) plus the one package installer `house.packages.sh`, which installs the layers' OS packages and the project's seeded `os-packages.txt` as ONE cached Docker layer, so a rebuild reinstalls nothing that has not changed (post-create runs the same installer: a no-op in a house-built image, the install in an adopted image of the project's own). `agent` brings `base:debian` + the Node feature, `node` swaps in `typescript-node`, and Firebase / voice / web / Angular add their own pieces. What must outlive a rebuild and is not an image layer lives in a persisted directory: `.claude` (a host bind), `~/.config`, `~/.local` and `~/.cache` (volumes). Chromium's system libraries are image packages too — projected from Playwright's own table for the pinned version by `tools/playwright-deps/project.mjs` (re-run with `--write` whenever `PLAYWRIGHT_VERSION` or the images' Debian moves; `tools/test-layers` fails on a stale projection). A tool Debian does not ship goes there too, pinned: an `osPackages` group may name the third-party apt `repository` it installs from (key dearmored into `/usr/share/keyrings/<id>.gpg`, `signed-by=` — never `apt-key`) and pin `name=version` (the firebase layer's `google-cloud-cli`); never a version-less devcontainer feature. The image's Node major is the PROJECT's `.nvmrc` (`_utils/node-version.ts`, seeded once with `HOUSE_NODE_MAJOR`) — never the Node of the machine running the upgrade.
  - **Every version a generator writes comes from one place, and nothing floats.** House pins live in `nx-tools/src/generators/_utils/versions.ts`; what is derived from npm (Angular major → `@angular/fire` → its own `firebase` range; Cloud Functions' GA Node runtimes for the pinned `firebase-tools`) is the generated `_utils/firebase-compat.ts`, projected by `node tools/firebase-compat/project.mjs [--write]`; Node's grammar facts (LTS codenames, the typescript-node majors that exist) are `_utils/node-facts.ts`, projected by `node tools/node-facts/project.mjs [--write]`. Both drift with UPSTREAM, so their checks run weekly (`.github/workflows/upstream-tables.yml`) and before every publish (`publish.sh`) — never in the per-push tests, where an upstream release would turn unrelated PRs red. Messages that rest on a table say "as of <date>": a project's toolkit holds a frozen copy. The floating rule is ONE function (`_utils/version-spec.ts`); every manifest write goes through `_utils/dependencies.ts` (`declareDependencies`, `updateManifest`), which refuse `latest`/`next`/`*`/unbounded specs, and the generator test HARNESS fails any case that writes a floating version into any package.json, whatever the write path. Moving a pin is a release decision with a migration for existing projects, which FREEZE every value they write and share only the pure mechanics that take values as parameters (`node-spec.ts`, `angularfire-judge.ts`). Those pure, import-free modules are also what `engine/house-probe.mts` loads (Node type stripping) so house.sh's preflight refuses an unresolvable Node or an unpairable `add-layer firebase` BEFORE anything is written — the generators' throw is the backstop.
  - **`new` is `add-layer` against an empty dir — literally.** The bootstrap is gated on the ensure set (closed under `requires`), never on layer names in the script: `node` ensured → `create-nx-workspace --preset=apps`, else `git init` + the same wrapper `nx init` an upgrade uses; each ensured layer's `nxPlugin` is `nx add`ed; the first app (`nx g @bespunky/nx-tools:app apps/<app> --stack=<adapter> --layers=<set>`) only when an ensured layer's adapter creates apps. Then the planner runs exactly as in an upgrade, `house-doc` last. This is what lets `house.sh add-layer agent <repo>` retrofit house DX onto *any* repo, this one included.
- **Adoption vs ownership.** `.devcontainer/.bespunky-devcontainer.json` marks a devcontainer this generator wrote. Absent it, an existing `devcontainer.json` is **merged additively** (never overwritten, comments preserved via `jsonc-parser` in-place edits — replacing an array wholesale destroys the comments between its members) and an existing `post-create.sh` is **left alone**, with the house script written beside it as `post-create.bespunky.sh`. An adopted devcontainer's own image source (`image`, `build`, …) is never joined by the house's `build` — that would be two image sources; it is recorded in `adopted.skipped` and the one-line switch printed, while `house.Dockerfile`/`house.packages.sh` are still written (inert until used) and post-create installs the packages instead. `post-create.local.sh` (any other setup) and `os-packages.txt` (OS packages) are the never-regenerated seams for a consumer's own.
- `nx-tools/` — `@bespunky/nx-tools`, the **house Nx generators** (TypeScript, Nx-devkit `Tree`-based — every config change is Nx-native, never a hand-rolled file edit). This is a **payload for house projects, not this repo's own build.**
- The *project-specific half* of a consumer CLAUDE.md is SEEDED by `house-doc` (`CLAUDE.seed.md.tpl`, layer-gated like the house docs) when the repo has none, and the skill fills its prompts. House guidance is **two generated, regenerable files** in the consumer project (never hand-edited there): **`HOUSE.rules.md`**, the always-on directives, which the generated pointer block **`@`-imports** so they load every session; and **`HOUSE.md`**, the mechanical how-to, which it links for on-demand reading. Claude Code follows `@` imports but does not load merely-linked files — so which of the two a rule lands in decides whether it is ever actually in context.

`skills/new/SKILL.md` is the orchestrator and the source of truth for the engine's sequence; the README's "How the engine works" mirrors it.

## `nx-tools` payload — build & publish

The generators live as TypeScript in the toolkit. Nx can't run raw TS from `node_modules`, so distribution is a separate step:
- Compile: `engine/compile-generators.mts` (reused by the publisher).
- Publish `@bespunky/nx-tools` to npm: `tools/publish-nx-tools/publish.sh` (validate first with `--dry-run`; **bump `engine/nx-tools/package.json` version first — and that bump is gated on the migrations question, see *Release & versioning* below**). Runs on the **local Node** when it's 22.18+ (the bar is type-stripping for `compile-generators.mts`), falling back to Docker otherwise — Docker was never the requirement, a modern Node was. Force the container with `--docker`. If npm 2FA is on, pass `--otp <code>`, or drop an npm **automation token** in `~/.npmrc` and it publishes unattended.
- **Publish fails on auth** (`ENEEDAUTH`/`401`/`E403`/missing `~/.npmrc`/expired OTP)? `tools/set-npm-token/set-npm-token.sh` writes an automation token into `~/.npmrc` so publishes run unattended. **The token stays private from Claude: do NOT ask for it in chat or run this script yourself** (the Bash tool is no interactive TTY, and a pasted token would leak into the transcript) — **tell the user to run the script in their own terminal** (silent prompt), then re-run the publish. See `tools/set-npm-token/README.md`.
- **CI auto-publishes on bump.** `.github/workflows/publish-nx-tools.yml` runs `publish.sh` on every push to `main` that touches the payload, but **only publishes when `engine/nx-tools/package.json`'s version isn't already on npm** — so a bump commit ships automatically and every other push is a no-op (it reuses the same script, so CI and hand-publishing can't drift). Auth is the `NPM_TOKEN` repo secret (an npm **automation** token, which bypasses 2FA). Publishing by hand is still the fallback when CI is unavailable.

`tools/extract-tool/` is the cross-workspace half of reusable-tool extraction (`extract-tool.sh --from <project> [--lib <lib>]`), also Docker-run. Background: `docs/reusable-tool-extraction.md`.

## Release & versioning

**Release a plugin with `nx release` — never by hand.** Every plugin is an Nx project (`plugins/<p>/project.json`, tagged `type:claude-plugin`), and `nx.json`'s `plugins` release group versions them independently:

```bash
nx release version --projects=<plugin-name> --specifier=patch|minor|major   # then commit
```

It writes `plugins/<p>/.claude-plugin/plugin.json` through a custom **`versionActions`** implementation (`tools/nx-release/plugin-version-actions.js` — Nx's documented seam for versioning a manifest that isn't a `package.json`), and then **derives `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json`** from the manifests in its `afterAllProjectsVersioned` hook. **The registry is generated: never hand-edit a version or description in it.** Both `version` and `description` are derived from the manifest (`source` is preserved) — edit a plugin's pitch in its `plugin.json`. **Descriptions have hard limits** because Claude Desktop (claude.ai) stores them truncated while Claude Code reads the full text, so an overrun is invisible from here: a plugin description ≤ 500 characters, a skill's frontmatter `description` ≤ 1024 with no `<` or `>`. `node tools/check-descriptions/check.mjs` enforces them (CI + the pre-push hook); the exhaustive per-skill catalog text belongs in `README.md` and the skill body, never in the trigger. The specifier is always explicit (`specifierSource: prompt`), so the house rule still holds: **any change to a plugin gets a bump**, including a README typo. Bumps land as dedicated `chore(release): bump …` commits. Consumers upgrade with `git pull` → `/plugin marketplace update claude-toolkit` → `/reload-plugins`.

**`minor` means minor — `adjustSemverBumpsForZeroMajorVersion: false` is set deliberately.** Nx **defaults that to `true`**, which, while a package's major is `0`, silently demotes every relative bump: `major` → `minor`, `minor` → `patch`. Everything here is `0.x`, so on the default `--specifier=minor` on `0.26.4` yields **`0.26.5`** — and the log still reads *"Applied semver relative bump `minor` … to get new version 0.26.5"*, because it echoes the specifier you asked for rather than the one it applied. That line is self-contradictory on its face and has already been misread once as a tooling bug. Nx's reasoning for the default is ordinary (a `0.x` package is pre-stable, so nothing is significant enough to move the second digit), but it disagrees with this repo's own practice: `0.24.0`, `0.25.0` and `0.26.0` were all hand-written second-digit releases from before `nx release` existed here, and under the default you could never *ask* for one with `minor`. So the mapping is turned off and the words mean what they say. Two consequences: `--specifier=major` now really does produce `1.0.0` (only ask for it if you mean it), and an exact version is always available as its own specifier — `nx release version --projects=<p> --specifier=0.27.0`.

**A missed plugin bump fails SILENTLY, which is why it is machine-checked.** A missed `@bespunky/nx-tools` bump is loud — CI skips the publish and the next upgrade installs the old payload. A missed *plugin* bump is not: the repo has the change, the marketplace advertises the old version, `/plugin marketplace update` is a no-op, and consumers stay behind forever with nothing to see. This repo shipped that bug twice — `bespunky-workflow` at `2c58e20`, then `bespunky-engineering` + `bespunky-design-system` — **both times from a sweep that crossed plugin boundaries while the commit was named after a different plugin.** That is the hazard: a repo-wide rename or ref-fix is one decision applied to N plugins, and the bump checklist fires on decisions.

So `tools/check-release-invariants/check.mjs` asks, after the fact, the question nobody remembers to: *did the thing that should have happened, happen?* It checks that every plugin (and the payload) whose **shipped content** moved since its last release was released again, that the derived registry still agrees with the manifests, and that no migration sits above the payload version. The rule itself — semver ordering and the ceiling — lives once in `tools/check-release-invariants/rules.cjs`, called by the checker, `publish.sh` and the publish workflow; `house.sh` keeps its own copy because it runs inside consumers' projects where this repo does not exist — a cross-reference comment in both is the whole mitigation, deliberately: the only way they can disagree is over prerelease ordering, and this repo has never published a prerelease. It runs in CI on every push (`.github/workflows/release-invariants.yml`) and as a **pre-push hook** (`tools/git-hooks/pre-push`, wired by `core.hooksPath` in `post-create.local.sh`; bypass with `--no-verify`). It **detects and reports — it never bumps**: patch vs minor is a judgment about what a change means to consumers.

**The migrations invariant: `max(version in migrations.json) <= version in engine/nx-tools/package.json`.** A migration is collected by `nx migrate` only when its declared version falls *within* the range it is walking — from the version the project has, up to the version being installed. Register a migration at a version the package hasn't reached and it sits above the ceiling forever: never collected, never run, and silent about it. So **adding a migration means bumping the payload's version in the same commit** — the migration's `version` field and `assets/nx-tools/package.json` are one decision, not two.

**And the gate runs the other way too: NO PAYLOAD RELEASE SHIPS WITHOUT ITS MIGRATIONS.** Before bumping `engine/nx-tools/package.json`, interrogate every change going out with one question — *does this alter a shape that projects already on disk have?* A renamed target, a relocated project or library, a retired config/environment file, a changed file shape a generator used to heal and no longer does, a moved path, a dropped option: each is a one-way delta, and **the release is not finished until a migration carries it**. "There is nothing to migrate" is a legitimate and common answer — a brand-new generator, a new layer, a fix to an owned template artifact that every upgrade regenerates anyway — but it is a **finding you reach deliberately, never a default you fall into**; when it *is* the answer, say so in the release commit message, so the next reader can tell a considered "nothing to migrate" from a forgotten one. Skipping a migration the release owed fails **silently and permanently**: existing projects install the new version, the ladder collects nothing, `house-doc` stamps them current — and the shape gap is now sealed behind a stamp every later sync believes.

**A migration CLEANS UP AFTER ITSELF — writing the new state is only half of it.** The migration is not done until the old state is *gone*, and this is where the ladder has actually drawn blood (see `dae4194`, which audited all eight migrations against a fixture carrying every legacy shape):

- **Delete what the new state replaces** — retired targets, configurations, orphaned files, duplicated declarations. A migration that only adds is how a workspace accumulates clutter nobody dares remove.
- **Retarget every reference to anything it moved.** A path move is a *rename*, so every occurrence of the old path **is** a reference to the thing that moved — including all the ones the toolkit never wrote: a jest `moduleNameMapper`, an eslint files glob, a `.vscode` `scss.includePaths`, a README. Rewriting them is mechanical, not clever; name each rewritten file in the log, since a migration lands as its own commit and stays reviewable on its own.
- **Ask what the move breaks by OMISSION, not only what it leaves stale.** The sharpest bug in that audit wasn't a dangling reference — it was `package.json` `workspaces` globs: `tools/*` had covered the design system, `packages/*` may not exist, so relocating the library silently dropped it out of the workspace entirely, surfacing nowhere near the cause.
- **Carrying data means clearing the original.** Copying a value to its new home and leaving the old copy behind is how two sources of truth are born — and "the generator overwrites that file moments later anyway" is not a defence, because the per-app generators are skipped whenever an upgrade can't resolve the app (`UPGRADE_PARTIAL`), which is exactly the run where the stale copy survives.
- **Where a deletion would be a GUESS, don't delete — but don't stay silent either: REPORT it.** A file whose name a project may legitimately use for its own purposes, or a declaration something else may still read, is not yours to remove on a hunch (removing a still-referenced declaration turns a duplicated value into a file that doesn't compile). Say what was left, name it, and say why. An unexplained leftover is indistinguishable from an oversight. **In a `devcontainer.json`, don't guess at all — ask `houseWrote()`** (`generators/_utils/devcontainer-provenance.ts`): an owned file is the house's, and in an adopted one the marker's `adopted.houseAdded` records exactly what the house's merge added (and still holds), so a migration may remove that and must report the rest. Projects adopted before 0.41.0 have no record for their earlier additions. **And "might be theirs" is not the test — "might something still depend on it" is.** A line the house has SUPERSEDED with a capability it now guarantees (0.40.0's `claude-code` feature, replaced by the native install first on PATH) can be depended on by nothing, so it goes whoever wrote it — gated on the guarantee being present (`0.43.0/remove-superseded-claude-code-feature`). Reporting it instead left a half-done job in exactly the projects that needed the fix.

**DOGFOOD EVERY PAYLOAD RELEASE BEFORE IT SHIPS — the finish gate, made concrete for this repo.** One bug (house containers froze Claude Code) took four payload releases in an afternoon (0.40.0 → 0.42.0 → 0.43.0 → 0.44.0), each a miss the user found by rebuilding and looking: a PATH entry built on `${containerEnv:HOME}` (empty in every container), a superseded feature left in adopted devcontainers, its pin left in `devcontainer-lock.json`. Fixtures passed every time, because a fixture encodes the author's assumption instead of testing it. So, before bumping `engine/nx-tools/package.json`:

1. **Sweep** — `git grep '<every identifier the change renames, removes or moves>'` over the whole repo; every hit, lock and generated files included, is handled in this release or left with a stated reason.
2. **Run the release the way a consumer receives it — on this repo AND on a consumer.** In a worktree, `house.sh upgrade --local .` (it packs the working tree), then read the WHOLE `git diff` the upgrade produced, not just the files you meant to change. Then `node tools/dogfood-consumer/run.mjs`: it walks both consumer roads in one step — a Firebase + Angular project built with the RELEASED toolkit, seeded with the shapes reporting projects grew, upgraded twice with this checkout (succeeds, then a no-op), built and linted; and a real `new --local` for every preset. This repo wears no `angular` or `firebase` layer, so its self-upgrade never runs those generators — and a `new --preset=angular --firebase` broken by the release under test once reached review because the hand dogfood only ever created its consumer with the released toolkit.
3. **When the change reaches the container** (devcontainer fragments, `post-create`, PATH, features), ask the user to rebuild from that worktree's branch and observe the outcome yourself (`which -a <tool>`, the env, the file) **before** the release — not after it.
4. Then release once.

## Common commands

**The product is still markdown — there is no build, lint or test for the skills.** But this repo now *dogfoods its own engine*: the `agent` layer has been added to it (then `scaffold.sh --sync --ensure=agent .`, today `house.sh add-layer agent .`), so it carries the `agent` layer (`HOUSE.md`, the devcontainer, `.claude/settings.json`, the window identity) and, underneath it, a minimal Nx workspace — `nx.json`, a root `package.json` and a lockfile. Nx is the *mechanism floor*: every house generator is an Nx-devkit generator invoked through `nx g`, so the DX layer cannot be applied without it. Those files exist to host the tooling, **not** to build the skills; there is still nothing to compile here.

Two consequences worth knowing:

- **`HOUSE.md` is generated — never hand-edit it.** It carries the house architecture directives and is rewritten by every upgrade. Repo-specific guidance (this file) stays here; `CLAUDE.md` holds only a generated pointer block to it.
- **The `SessionStart` version hook stays silent in this repo**, by design: it exempts a project whose `CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT` lives inside it, because the "installed" plugin *is* the working tree being edited, so comparing versions would be comparing the file to itself.

The dev loop:

| Task | How |
| --- | --- |
| Load your working-tree skills into a session | `claude plugin marketplace add .` (the devcontainer's post-create does this on build) |
| Pick up mid-session skill edits | `/reload-plugins` (or `/plugin marketplace update claude-toolkit` if added from GitHub) |
| Release a plugin | `nx release version --projects=<name> --specifier=patch` — writes `plugin.json` **and** derives `marketplace.json`; never hand-edit either |
| Check the release invariants | `node tools/check-release-invariants/check.mjs` (also CI + the pre-push hook) |
| Check description limits | `node tools/check-descriptions/check.mjs` — plugin ≤ 500, skill ≤ 1024 and no `<` `>` (what claude.ai stores; also CI + the pre-push hook) |
| Check that every shebang can run | `node tools/check-script-modes/check.mjs` — a tracked file declaring `#!` must be executable (also CI + the pre-push hook). Exemptions are predicates with reasons *inside the checker*, printed on every run; add one there, never by loosening the rule |
| Test the voice plugin's conversation logic | `node tools/test-voice/run.mjs` — phrasing, reply understanding, the `ask_by_voice` server (live transcript, repeat, cancel, supersede) and the speaker, against fake audio scripts (node + bash; also CI). The voice band mod: `claude plugin validate plugins/voice` + `claude plugin test plugins/voice` (needs the `claude` CLI, so not CI). The audio boundaries themselves (`speak.sh`, `listen.sh`) are exercised by hand |
| Test the spinner-tips engine | `node tools/test-tips/run.mjs` — the tips hook's promises about the user's settings file (node only; also CI) |
| Project / check the mod brand | `node tools/mod-brand/project.mjs [--write]` — the one toolkit look for mods (`tools/mod-brand/brand.tsx`: the `✦ bespunky` mark, accent, `BrandFrame`, `BrandDivider`, `BrandCommandRow`, `brandLine`) copied into every plugin whose `hooks.json` names `modules`, as `hooks/_brand.tsx`; the check fails on drift, an orphan copy, or a mod typing the glyph itself. `--write` after any brand change or a new mod plugin. Tests: `node tools/test-mod-brand/run.mjs` (node only; also CI) |
| Test the engine's guards | `bash tools/test-scaffold/run.sh` — the refusals whose regression would be **silent** (~1s, bash + git only; also CI) |
| Test the layer registry | `node tools/test-layers/run.mjs` — projection drift (`engine/layers.sh` vs the registry), plans, presets, the agent artifacts; `--write` regenerates `layers.sh` after a descriptor or preset change (also CI) |
| Test the migrations | `node tools/test-migrations/run.mjs` — fixture workspaces run through the compiled rungs; idempotence is asserted by the harness for every case (needs `yarn install`; also CI, deliberately **not** the pre-push hook). Add a case: one file in `tools/test-migrations/cases/`, no wiring |
| Test the generators | `node tools/test-generators/run.mjs` — the compiled generators and their seams (layout, linking, project files) against fixture workspaces in every layout × linking cell; idempotence asserted by the harness for every case, a one-way case opts out with a printed `once:` reason. Cases needing `@nx/js` / `@nx/angular` (optional peers, not devDependencies) skip and are counted; `--strict` fails them (needs `yarn install`; also CI). Add a case: one file in `tools/test-generators/cases/`, shapes from `workspaces.mjs`. Shares its compile/fixture machinery with the migration and layer tests (`tools/test-support/payload.mjs`) |
| Run the Angular TS-solution tripwire | `bash tools/test-angular-ts-solution/run.sh` — a real `--preset=ts` workspace, the house Angular adapter, `nx sync` + typecheck + build (network, ~5–15 min; `KEEP=1` keeps the workspace). Guards the **undocumented** `NX_IGNORE_UNSUPPORTED_TS_SETUP` opt-out; CI runs it weekly and on Angular-adapter/linking changes, deliberately **not** on every push or in the pre-push hook |
| Run the firebase-tools tripwire | `node tools/test-firebase-tools/run.mjs` — the pinned firebase-tools, for real: the dotenv parser `tools/emulator-secrets.cjs` ports, the **undocumented** `CLOUD_SECRET_MANAGER_URL` sink, and the Functions emulator end to end under the offline `demo-` id (network, ~1–3 min; `FIREBASE_TOOLS_CACHE=<dir>` reuses an install). CI runs it weekly and on emulator-safety/version changes; **re-run it on every `FIREBASE_TOOLS_VERSION` bump** |
| Validate the nx-tools payload | `tools/publish-nx-tools/publish.sh --dry-run` |
| Dogfood a payload release as a consumer | `node tools/dogfood-consumer/run.mjs [--released=<ref>] [--toolkit=<path>] [--only=<steps>] [--keep]` — released-toolkit Firebase + Angular consumer → seeded shapes (data, `SEEDS`) → `upgrade --local` twice (OK, then a no-op) → build + lint; plus `new --local` for every preset. PASS/FAIL table, logs kept (network, ~20–40 min; deliberately **not** CI or the pre-push hook) |
| Publish nx-tools | ask the migrations question (*Release & versioning*), write any migration it owes, **dogfood it** (sweep · `house.sh upgrade --local .` in a worktree + read the whole diff · `tools/dogfood-consumer/run.mjs` · a rebuild when it reaches the container), bump `engine/nx-tools/package.json`, then `tools/publish-nx-tools/publish.sh` |
| Create a project with the engine | `bash plugins/house/engine/house.sh new [--preset=<id>] [--add-layer=<csv>] <project> [app]` |
| Upgrade a project | `… /house.sh upgrade <project-path>` (adds no layer) |
| Add a layer / retrofit a project | `… /house.sh add-layer [--firebase] <layers-csv> <project-path>` |
| Test an nx-tools change before publishing | add `--local` to any of the above — it packs the working tree and installs *that* instead of the registry copy |

## Conventions

- **Skills are the product; the frontmatter `description` is the trigger.** Invest there.
- **Router skills:** SKILL.md indexes, `reference/*.md` holds the depth — don't inline reference material back into SKILL.md.
- **Every tool a layer brings into the container is audited for what must survive a rebuild — in the same change.** A rebuild throws away everything outside a mount, so a tool added without this question silently costs every consumer a re-login (or a re-setup) on every rebuild, forever, and nobody notices until they are annoyed enough to ask (`docs/features/2026-10-06-persist-auth/`). So whenever a fragment gains a `features` entry, an `osPackages` group, a `postCreate` piece or an image (an OS package belongs in `osPackages` — a cached image layer — never in a `postCreate` apt step, which reinstalls it on every rebuild): find where the tool keeps its **state** — logins and tokens first, then config, then anything expensive to rebuild — by running it and looking, not by assuming. Then solve it right away, preferring the **fewest, least specific entrypoints**: the tool keeps its state under `~/.config`, installs under `~/.local` or caches under `~/.cache` (the XDG homes, each one persisted volume in `agent`) → nothing to do; it has its own dir but honours an env var → point it at a persisted location (`CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`); it writes a file `$HOME` keeps container-local (`~/.gitconfig`) → re-derive it in a `postCreate` piece; only when none of those fit, a new mount — for the **directory**, never one per file or per tool, unless that directory must not be kept whole. "Nothing to keep" is a legitimate answer, but a deliberate one: say it in the commit message, the same way a release says "nothing to migrate". And extend `tools/test-layers`' persistence case with whatever was added.
- **Extending the engine is generator work:** add or modify an `@bespunky/nx-tools` generator (Nx-devkit `Tree`) — never hand-write file edits into `house.sh`. A literal `angular-*` Nx preset forces a demo app, so the scaffold path is the `apps` preset + `nx add @nx/angular` + a `--minimal` app.
- **Every migration gets a fixture case.** `node tools/test-migrations/run.mjs` runs the compiled rungs against `@nx/devkit` `Tree` workspaces built to the shape each one will actually meet. It exists because a migration writes into someone else's repo, once, unattended — and its throwaway ancestor caught five defects in one rung that four reading passes had missed, including a walk that would have edited another git worktree's source. Add the case in the same commit as the rung. **And a rung that skips "already migrated" input lists every shape an earlier release shipped carrying the marker it skips on, as the case's `historicalShapes`** (taken from git, sha named): the harness asserts each converges to the canonical result or states why not — idempotence alone never sees them, which is how 0.24.3 left a 0.7.1-repaired interface half-migrated for good.
- **A one-way change is a MIGRATION, not healing code in a generator.** "The old shape becomes the new shape" (a renamed target, a relocated project, a retired config) belongs in `src/migrations/<version>/`, bumped with the payload. Generators state *desired state* for what they own; they no longer carry the history of every shape the toolkit has shipped. **A migration is only done when the old shape is gone** — deleted, its references retargeted, its duplicates cleared, and anything deliberately left behind *reported*. Both halves of that rule — *every release ships the migrations it owes*, and *every migration cleans up after itself* — are stated in full under **Release & versioning** above; read it before you bump the payload version.
- **Adding a plugin needs four things:** its `plugin.json`, a `project.json` tagged `type:claude-plugin` (this is what makes it a release target — without it `nx release` cannot see it and the invariants checker will not guard it), an entry in `marketplace.json`, and a row in `README.md`. Its **version** is then only ever written by `nx release`. Give it a `tips.txt` too, or it never shows up in the spinner tips.
- **Every toolkit mod wears the brand.** A pane, band, status entry or toast imports from its plugin's generated `hooks/_brand.tsx` — `BrandFrame` for drawn sites, `BrandCommandRow` for a slash command's output row, `brandLine()` for a status entry or toast (Claude Code already titles both with the plugin's name, so the glyph alone) — and never re-types the mark or colour; change the look once in `tools/mod-brand/brand.tsx` and `--write`.
- **Every plugin owns its spinner tips in `tips.txt` at its root** (one per line, `#` comments). The `bespunky` plugin's `SessionStart` hook (`hooks/tips.mjs`) collects them from the toolkit plugins installed for the project and rotates a few into the user's `spinnerTipsOverride`. A plugin's own `settings.json` cannot set that key, so the hook is a guest in the user's settings file: it touches only the strings it wrote, never rewrites a file it can't parse, and never writes to stdout, because SessionStart stdout reaches the model. Those promises are tested by `node tools/test-tips/run.mjs` (also CI). When you add or change a capability, add or change its tip in the same commit. Keep a tip glanceable, and make sure any command it names actually works.
- **Never hand-edit a version.** `marketplace.json` is derived from the plugin manifests; editing it directly creates the exact drift the derivation exists to make impossible.

## General Guidelines for working with Nx

- For navigating/exploring the workspace, invoke the `nx-workspace` skill first - it has patterns for querying projects, targets, and dependencies
- When running tasks (for example build, lint, test, e2e, etc.), always prefer running the task through `nx` (i.e. `nx run`, `nx run-many`, `nx affected`) instead of using the underlying tooling directly
- Prefix nx commands with the workspace's package manager (e.g., `pnpm nx build`, `npm exec nx test`) - avoids using globally installed CLI
- You have access to the Nx MCP server and its tools, use them to help the user
- For Nx plugin best practices, check `node_modules/@nx/<plugin>/PLUGIN.md`. Not all plugins have this file - proceed without it if unavailable.
- NEVER guess CLI flags - always check nx_docs or `--help` first when unsure

## Scaffolding & Generators

- For scaffolding tasks (creating apps, libs, project structure, setup), ALWAYS invoke the `nx-generate` skill FIRST before exploring or calling MCP tools

## When to use nx_docs

- USE for: advanced config options, unfamiliar flags, migration guides, plugin configuration, edge cases
- DON'T USE for: basic generator syntax (`nx g @nx/react:app`), standard commands, things you already know
- The `nx-generate` skill handles generator discovery internally - don't call nx_docs just to look up generator syntax
